definition: Dispel means to drive away or scatter completely, especially a feeling, doubt, rumor, or myth.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dispel. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dispel should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum guide was quick to dispel the popular myth that bats are blind.
Easing a worry only softens it, while dispelling a worry drives it away completely.
Eradicate is even stronger and more sweeping than dispel; you dispel a doubt or a myth, but you eradicate a disease or a deep-rooted problem.

To banish is to drive something away as if by decree - you banish a thought, a worry, or a courtier, forcing it out. What is banished still exists somewhere, just not here. To dispel is to scatter a doubt, fear, or myth until nothing of it remains anywhere, usually with facts and explanations.

To erase is to remove all trace of something recorded or visible - marks, files, footage. Dispel works on live, floating things: moods, doubts, rumors, myths. You erase what was written down; you dispel what hangs in the air. A false belief is dispelled by evidence, not rubbed out.

To eliminate is the general word for getting rid of anything entirely - errors, suspects, weeds - and it says nothing about how. Dispel is specific: it scatters intangible things like fear, doubt, or a myth, and it works through explanation or evidence. You eliminate a problem; you dispel the worry surrounding it.

Dispel means to drive away or scatter completely, especially a feeling, doubt, rumor, or myth.
Visitors kept skipping the old lighthouse tour because of rumors that it was haunted.
The tour guide dispelled those fears by walking each group through every room and explaining the creaks and drafts one by one.
Bookings doubled within a month.
The guide did not wait for the fears to fade on their own; she actively and completely drove them away with explanations, which is exactly what dispel means.
Dispel is active and complete: a person or a piece of evidence deliberately drives away a doubt, fear, rumor, or myth.
Unlike dissipate, which describes something fading gradually on its own, dispelling is done on purpose.

It is also distinct from disperse, which describes a crowd or group physically scattering in different directions; dispel is reserved for intangible things like feelings and beliefs, never for crowds.

Every child in Port Alma grew up on the story: the old lighthouse was cursed, and any boat that passed too close would lose its engine.
Sailors traded the tale so confidently that some captains added a mile to their routes rather than test it.
Then a retired engineer named Ines Farro set out to dispel the legend the only way she trusted -- with records.
She published sixty years of harbor logs showing engine failures scattered evenly across the bay, no thicker near the light than anywhere else.
The story did not survive the chart.
Within a season, even the oldest captains steered straight past the tower without a second glance.
